messages.content: I want to develop a semantic parser that generalizes variable binding and quantifier scope to unseen compositions without sacrificing accuracy on familiar constructions. The targets are at least 90% logical-form exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations, with matched vocabulary and length distributions, and familiar-construction exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an equally sized supervised baseline.

That sets two conditions for the parser. It needs to handle withheld combinations of scope and binding with ≥90% logical-form exact match, while keeping familiar-construction exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of the equally sized supervised baseline. The goal is generalization to new compositions without losing the accuracy associated with familiar ones.
What does “unseen compositions” mean here? Does it mean the words themselves have to be new?

No. The specified test concerns withheld scope–binding combinations, while vocabulary and length distributions are matched. The intended novelty is in how the relevant constructions are combined, not a requirement to interpret unfamiliar words or unusually long inputs.
Can you distinguish quantifier scope from variable binding in ordinary terms?

Quantifier scope concerns which quantified expression is interpreted within the reach of another. Variable binding concerns which expression supplies the value for a dependent variable or reference. A semantic parser needs to represent these relationships in its logical form, rather than merely recognizing the words or constructions individually.
Could you give a small illustration without implying anything about the actual test items?

As a general illustration, “Every student read a book” can raise a scope question: is there one book shared across the students, or can the book vary by student? In “Every student praised herself,” interpreting “herself” involves a binding relationship with “every student.” These are illustrations of the concepts, not claims about which sentences or readings appear in the withheld combinations.
Why specify matched vocabulary and length distributions?

It keeps the stated target focused on scope–binding composition rather than making success depend on a different vocabulary or a different distribution of input lengths. Matching those distributions does not, by itself, establish that every other property is identical. The requirement specifically names vocabulary and length as the matched conditions.
Is the 90% threshold for all inputs, or for the withheld combinations?

It is for logical-form exact match on the withheld scope–binding combinations, under the stated matched-vocabulary and matched-length conditions. Familiar constructions have a separate accuracy requirement relative to the supervised baseline.
And is 90% included in “at least 90%”?
Yes. A score of exactly 90% meets the ≥90% threshold; a score below 90% does not.
What exactly is being compared on the familiar constructions?

Familiar-construction exact-match accuracy is compared with the exact-match accuracy of an equally sized supervised baseline. The requested margin is within two percentage points. That comparison is separate from the absolute ≥90% target for withheld scope–binding combinations.
Why say percentage points rather than percent?

Percentage points refer to a direct difference between accuracy percentages. For example, if a baseline accuracy were 94%, an accuracy of 92% would be two percentage points lower, while 91% would be three points lower. That example only illustrates the unit; it is not a stated baseline result.
Does “equally sized” tell us what kind of supervision the new parser must use?

No. The node identifies an equally sized supervised baseline as the familiar-construction comparator, but it does not prescribe the new parser’s method. It also does not specify here which dimension of size is meant, so there is no basis for replacing “equally sized” with a more particular claim about examples, parameters, or budget.
Suppose a parser did well on familiar constructions but fell below the threshold on withheld combinations. Would that meet this goal?

No. Both conditions matter: the ≥90% logical-form exact-match target on withheld scope–binding combinations and the two-percentage-point familiar-construction comparison. Strong familiar-construction accuracy alone would not satisfy the withheld-combination target.
And a strong withheld-combination score would not make the familiar-construction comparison optional?

Correct. The goal explicitly couples generalization with preserving accuracy on familiar constructions. Meeting the withheld-combination threshold would not remove the separate comparison with the equally sized supervised baseline.
Does logical-form exact match just mean the parser gets roughly the intended meaning?

No. Exact match is a stricter criterion than a broad judgment that a prediction conveys roughly the right meaning: the predicted logical form must match the reference under the evaluation’s matching convention. The goal does not specify that convention or say that merely equivalent-looking outputs receive credit.
Does the goal commit us to a particular parser architecture or training procedure?

It does not. It states the capability sought and the two accuracy requirements, but not an architecture, a training procedure, or a claimed result. Those details should not be inferred from the target alone.
So how would you state the aim in one careful sentence?

Develop a semantic parser that generalizes variable binding and quantifier scope to unseen compositions, achieves ≥90% logical-form exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations with matched vocabulary and length distributions, and keeps familiar-construction exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an equally sized supervised baseline.
For the parser we discussed, I propose training a parameter-matched, typed scope-sketch decoder with de Bruijn binding and a template-gated supervised fallback for familiar constructions.

That is a proposed approach, not a claim that the accuracy targets have been reached. It combines a typed scope-sketch decoder for representing scope structure, de Bruijn binding for bound-variable references, and a template-gated supervised fallback intended for familiar constructions. “Parameter-matched” adds a size constraint to the proposed model comparison.
What would a scope sketch represent, in broad terms?

A scope sketch can be understood as a structural outline of how quantified expressions relate in scope, before treating the finished logical form as just an undifferentiated output string. In this proposal, the decoder would produce that kind of structured representation. The proposal does not specify a sketch notation or decoding procedure.
And what does “typed” add to the proposal?

It indicates that the scope-sketch decoder should respect types in the representation it produces. Conceptually, typing helps distinguish structurally appropriate combinations from ones that do not fit their expected roles. The node does not define a particular type system or say how typing would be enforced during training or decoding.
I want to be clear about de Bruijn binding. Is that a different name for quantifier scope?

No. Quantifier scope concerns the arrangement and interpretation of quantified expressions. De Bruijn notation concerns how bound-variable references are represented: instead of depending on arbitrary variable names, a reference can identify its binder by its position or nesting relationship. Both matter to a logical form, but they address different aspects of its structure.
Can you make the point about variable names a little more concrete?

In a named-variable representation, changing a bound variable from, say, x to y need not change the underlying binding relationship, provided its bound occurrences change consistently. A de Bruijn representation expresses that relationship through binder position rather than the choice of name. That is the motivation for describing this proposal as using de Bruijn binding; no particular indexing convention is specified here.
Does using de Bruijn binding guarantee generalization to new scope–binding combinations?

No. It specifies a way to represent binding, not a guaranteed accuracy result. The proposal is aimed at the goal of generalizing to withheld scope–binding combinations, but whether the trained parser reaches ≥90% logical-form exact match would still have to be established. The representation alone does not settle that question.
Where does the supervised fallback fit?

The proposed fallback is for familiar constructions. “Template-gated” says that templates govern when the supervised fallback is used, while the typed scope-sketch decoder remains part of the proposed approach. The proposal does not state what the templates are, how the gate identifies a familiar construction, or how conflicts between possible outputs would be resolved.
So the fallback is there because the familiar-construction requirement matters too?

That is the role it serves in the proposal: it addresses the aim of retaining exact-match accuracy on familiar constructions while pursuing generalization through the scope-sketch and binding representation. It should not be read as evidence that familiar accuracy will stay within two percentage points of the equally sized supervised baseline; that remains a target.
Does “template-gated” mean every sentence matching a template is necessarily interpreted correctly?

No. It describes a proposed way of controlling access to the supervised fallback, not a correctness guarantee. The node makes no claim about a template’s coverage, the reliability of a match, or the accuracy of a fallback output.
Would it be accurate to call this one plain supervised decoder with a new output notation?

That would omit parts of the proposal. It calls for a typed scope-sketch decoder, de Bruijn binding, and a template-gated supervised fallback for familiar constructions. The node does not spell out their detailed integration, so it is better to name the components than to reduce them to a particular architecture that has not been specified.
How should I read “parameter-matched” alongside the earlier comparison to an equally sized supervised baseline?

“Parameter-matched” makes the proposed model’s parameter count part of the comparison constraint. The goal’s familiar-construction requirement compares exact-match accuracy with an equally sized supervised baseline. The proposal does not give parameter counts or further comparison details, so it would be premature to claim a particular numerical match or any accuracy outcome.
Does parameter matching also mean the training data and computational cost are matched?

Not from this proposal. Matching parameters does not, on its own, specify identical training data, training time, or computational cost. Those would be additional conditions, and they are not stated here.
Could you connect the pieces without filling in a training recipe?

At the conceptual level, the typed scope-sketch decoder is the proposed means of producing structured scope interpretations; de Bruijn binding provides a way to express which binder a variable reference belongs to; and the template-gated supervised fallback is intended to handle familiar constructions. Training that parameter-matched combination is the proposal. Nothing here specifies an objective, a data-generation scheme, a gate rule, or a sequence of training stages.
If I describe the fallback as a proven safeguard against losing familiar-construction accuracy, is that too strong?

Yes. It is a proposed mechanism directed at that concern, not a proven safeguard. The familiar-construction criterion remains exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an equally sized supervised baseline, and this proposal does not report a measurement against it.
Likewise, should I avoid saying the scope-sketch decoder already solves the withheld combinations?

Yes. The proposal does not report results on withheld scope–binding combinations. Its intended purpose is consistent with the ≥90% logical-form exact-match goal under matched vocabulary and length distributions, but intent and measured performance are different things.
Give me a concise formulation that keeps it a proposal.

Propose training a parameter-matched, typed scope-sketch decoder that represents binding with de Bruijn notation and uses a template-gated supervised fallback for familiar constructions, as an approach to the stated scope–binding generalization and familiar-accuracy goals.
Can the template gate distinguish withheld scope–binding combinations from familiar ones when vocabulary and sentence length are matched?

The proposal does not establish that it can. Matching vocabulary and length distributions removes two possible shortcuts, but it does not rule out a distinction based on the scope–binding composition itself. Whether the gate can make that distinction depends on what its templates recognize, which has not been specified.
So matched vocabulary and length do not make the two kinds of input indistinguishable?

Not necessarily. Inputs can have similar words and lengths while differing in how their constructions combine. The question is whether the gate has access to a reliable indication of that compositional difference. The stated matching conditions alone cannot answer that.
Would a gate that relied just on word choice or sentence length be enough?

Those would not provide a dependable basis for the intended distinction under the stated matching conditions. The withheld combinations are defined by scope and binding, not by a requirement for different vocabulary or longer sentences. That does not mean every possible gate must fail; it means success cannot be inferred from lexical or length cues.
Is recognizing a familiar template the same as knowing a combination was withheld?

No. A template match is whatever the gate’s specified matching rule says it is. It would only serve as a distinction between familiar and withheld combinations if that rule aligned with the relevant scope–binding compositions. Calling the gate “template-gated” does not itself establish such alignment.
Could a template include structural information rather than just words?

Conceptually, yes: a template could describe aspects of a construction’s structure. But the proposal does not say what information these templates encode or how the gate uses it. Structural templates might make the distinction possible; their mere inclusion would not guarantee it.
I’m trying to separate what is possible in principle from what this proposal actually claims.

In principle, matched vocabulary and length distributions leave room for a gate to use information about composition. In this proposal, however, there is no defined gate rule or evidence of its performance. So the careful answer is neither that matching makes discrimination impossible nor that the proposed gate has demonstrated it.
What if the gate matches a familiar-looking part of an input, but the overall scope–binding combination is withheld?

That illustrates the central uncertainty. Recognizing a familiar component is not necessarily the same as recognizing the full combination. If a gate treated a partial match as sufficient to invoke the supervised fallback, it might not distinguish the withheld composition from a familiar one. Whether that situation arises depends on the unspecified templates and matching rule.
And could being too restrictive cause the opposite issue?

Potentially. If a gate failed to recognize a familiar construction, it would not route that case to the familiar-construction fallback as intended. Those are conditional concerns about how a gate could behave, not reported errors or evidence that either issue occurs.
Does the word “withheld” imply the gate gets a label telling it which examples were withheld?

No. “Withheld” describes the scope–binding combinations in the stated evaluation condition. Nothing in the proposal says the gate receives a withheld-versus-familiar label for an input. Its ability to make that distinction therefore cannot be assumed from the term alone.
Then what is the narrow answer to my original question?

It may be possible if the templates capture the relevant scope–binding composition, but the proposal does not specify enough to tell whether the template gate can reliably distinguish withheld combinations from familiar ones. Matched vocabulary and length distributions make lexical and length shortcuts insufficient; they do not settle what a structurally informed gate could do.
Here is a hypothesis about the gate: typed scope–binder signatures will route at least 95% of withheld combinations to sketch decoding and at least 98% of familiar examples to fallback.

That gives the earlier gate question two explicit, testable routing predictions. The hypothesis is that typed scope–binder signatures will send ≥95% of withheld scope–binding combinations to sketch decoding and ≥98% of familiar examples to the supervised fallback. Those are predicted routing rates, not measured results or logical-form accuracy scores.
How does that address my concern about matching vocabulary and sentence length?

It proposes using typed scope–binder signatures as the basis for routing, rather than relying on differences in vocabulary or length. The hypothesis is that those signatures will distinguish the relevant compositions well enough to achieve the two stated routing rates even when vocabulary and sentence length are matched. It does not yet demonstrate that they do.
When you say “scope–binder signature,” what is the cautious way to understand that phrase?

As a proposed characterization of an input’s scope and binding structure, with type information included. The hypothesis names that characterization as the gate’s distinguishing signal. It does not specify a signature format, how signatures are obtained, or the exact rule that maps them to a route.
Is the 95% figure for the withheld combinations being sent to fallback?
No. For withheld combinations, the hypothesized direction is to sketch decoding, at a rate of at least 95%. The other figure is for familiar examples: at least 98% are hypothesized to go to fallback.
Does this mean the two percentages are calculated over the same set of examples?

No. They refer to different groups. The ≥95% prediction concerns withheld combinations, while the ≥98% prediction concerns familiar examples. Neither number is an overall routing percentage across both groups.
Would getting those routing rates mean the parser has achieved the original exact-match targets?

Not by itself. Routing an example to sketch decoding or fallback says which path handles it; it does not say whether that path produces the correct logical form. The original targets concern ≥90% logical-form exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations and familiar-construction exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an equally sized supervised baseline. The hypothesis here concerns routing, not those output accuracies.
Could the gate route a withheld example to sketch decoding and the parser still get it wrong?

Yes. Correct routing in the sense predicted by this hypothesis would not guarantee a correct logical form. The ≥95% figure says how often withheld combinations are expected to reach sketch decoding, not how often sketch decoding is expected to solve them.
The same applies to familiar examples reaching fallback?

Yes. The ≥98% figure predicts that familiar examples reach fallback; it does not guarantee their exact-match accuracy once there. Routing and interpretation are related parts of the proposed system, but they are different claims.
Should I interpret “at least” literally for both numbers?

Yes. The hypothesis includes 95% as meeting the withheld-to-sketch threshold and 98% as meeting the familiar-to-fallback threshold. It does not require those rates to be exactly 95% and 98%, and it does not assert that either has been observed.
Does the hypothesis tell us what happens to every example that is not routed as predicted?

No. It specifies the predicted proportions sent to the named destinations, but it does not detail all other routing outcomes or their consequences. We should not fill in unspecified behavior merely from the two thresholds.
Why mention types here rather than just saying the gate uses scope and binding?

Because “typed” is part of the proposed signal: the hypothesis specifically concerns typed scope–binder signatures. In broad terms, type information may help characterize structural roles, but the hypothesis does not say which types are represented or prove that type information is what makes the predicted rates attainable.
So is this a confident answer that the gate can distinguish the combinations?

It is a specific hypothesis about how well the gate will distinguish them, not a confirmed answer. It predicts ≥95% routing of withheld combinations to sketch decoding and ≥98% routing of familiar examples to fallback using typed scope–binder signatures. Whether those predictions hold remains unstated.
Can you state the hypothesis in one sentence while keeping that distinction clear?

The hypothesis is that typed scope–binder signatures will route at least 95% of withheld scope–binding combinations to sketch decoding and at least 98% of familiar examples to the supervised fallback, even with vocabulary and sentence length matched; those figures describe proposed routing performance, not established accuracy.

I want to turn the gate question into a test. The plan is to construct vocabulary- and length-matched ScopeBind-Match splits, train the typed-signature gate, and test for at least 95% withheld-sketch recall and at least 98% familiar-fallback specificity.

That is a plan for evaluating whether the gate distinguishes the two kinds of composition under the stated matching conditions. ScopeBind-Match provides the vocabulary- and length-matched splits; the typed-signature gate is trained; then its routing is tested against two thresholds: ≥95% withheld-sketch recall and ≥98% familiar-fallback specificity. The plan does not report that any of those steps has been completed or that either threshold has been reached.
Can you unpack “withheld-sketch recall” without changing what is being measured?

It is the proportion of withheld scope–binding combinations that the gate routes to sketch decoding. The planned test asks whether that proportion is at least 95%. It measures routing to the sketch path, not whether the resulting logical forms are correct.
And “familiar-fallback specificity”?

Here it is the proportion of familiar examples that the gate routes to fallback. The planned threshold is at least 98%. The denominator is the familiar examples, whereas withheld-sketch recall uses the withheld combinations as its denominator.
Why give the two routes separate measures rather than one overall routing score?

A single overall score could hide how the gate behaves on either group. These two planned measures separately ask whether withheld combinations reach sketch decoding at the specified rate and whether familiar examples reach fallback at its specified rate. Both thresholds are part of the plan; one does not stand in for the other.
Does “specificity” imply that familiar examples are somehow wrong or less important?
No. It is a label for the familiar-to-fallback routing measure in this plan, not a judgment about the examples. Familiar-construction accuracy remains important to the broader parser goal.
What role does ScopeBind-Match play?

ScopeBind-Match is the name given to the planned splits. They are to be matched for vocabulary and length so the gate’s routing can be tested on withheld and familiar scope–binding compositions without relying on those distributions being different. The plan does not provide a construction recipe or other split specifications.
Does matching mean every withheld sentence must have an identically worded, identically long familiar sentence?

That is not specified. The plan says the ScopeBind-Match splits will be vocabulary- and length-matched; it does not define matching as one-to-one pairing or require identical wording. It would be adding a constraint to treat that particular matching procedure as decided.
Could I say the matching proves that only scope and binding differ?

No. Matching vocabulary and length addresses those two distributions. It does not, by itself, establish that all other properties are held constant. The test is aimed at the scope–binding distinction, but the stated matching conditions should not be expanded into a stronger claim.
Where in the plan is the gate actually trained?

Training the typed-signature gate is the step between constructing the ScopeBind-Match splits and testing the routing thresholds. The plan does not specify its training objective, the signature format, or how examples are allocated for training and testing.
Is the typed-signature gate the same thing as the complete semantic parser?

No. In this plan, the gate determines routing between sketch decoding and fallback. Testing its routing does not test every part of the semantic parser’s output behavior. Even a case sent down the intended route could yield an incorrect logical form.
How does this plan get at the question of whether the gate can distinguish withheld combinations from familiar ones?

It makes that question measurable. After constructing the matched splits and training the gate, the test asks whether withheld combinations are sent to sketch decoding at least 95% of the time and familiar examples are sent to fallback at least 98% of the time. Those group-specific routing rates would address the distinction the question asks about; the plan itself supplies no measured answer.
If the vocabulary and length distributions are matched, does that make the test impossible for the gate?

Not necessarily. Matching those distributions limits reliance on vocabulary or length differences, but the plan tests whether typed signatures can guide routing based on the relevant compositions. Whether they can do so at the stated rates is precisely what remains to be tested.
What if a withheld combination contains pieces that are familiar individually?

The planned withheld-sketch recall still concerns the whole withheld combination: was it routed to sketch decoding? The plan does not say how the typed signature represents familiar pieces within a new combination, so we cannot predict that case’s route from the plan alone.
And the familiar-fallback measure asks about the whole familiar example, not just whether the gate spotted one familiar word?

Right. The measure counts familiar examples routed to fallback. It does not equate a familiar word, by itself, with a successful routing decision, and the plan does not specify the gate’s matching rule.
Can I treat exactly 95% recall and exactly 98% specificity as passing the planned tests?
Yes. Both are stated as minimum thresholds: ≥95% withheld-sketch recall and ≥98% familiar-fallback specificity. Exactly 95% or 98%, respectively, meets the corresponding threshold.
Would a result of 97% withheld-sketch recall tell me that familiar-fallback specificity also passes?

No. The measures have different denominators and different routing destinations. A withheld-sketch recall result, whatever its value, does not supply the familiar-fallback specificity result. The plan calls for testing both.
Should I describe either threshold as logical-form exact-match accuracy?

No. Both are gate-routing thresholds. Logical-form exact match concerns the parser’s output, while these measures concern which decoding path the gate selects. The broader parser goal has its own exact-match requirements, but this plan tests the gate’s routing distinction.
Could the test establish that the complete parser preserves accuracy on familiar constructions?

Not from these routing measures alone. Familiar examples reaching fallback at the planned rate would not tell us whether the fallback’s logical forms meet the familiar-construction exact-match comparison. This plan specifies a gate test, not a reported end-to-end accuracy result.
What is the most careful short statement of the plan?

Construct vocabulary- and length-matched ScopeBind-Match splits, train the typed-signature gate, and test whether it achieves ≥95% withheld-sketch recall and ≥98% familiar-fallback specificity. Those are planned routing tests, not completed results or substitutes for logical-form accuracy.
The next activity is to train the typed-signature gate on ScopeBind-Match and measure withheld-sketch recall and familiar-fallback specificity on matched test splits.

That puts the gate-routing question into an activity: train the typed-signature gate on ScopeBind-Match, then measure its routing on matched test splits. Withheld-sketch recall concerns withheld combinations sent to sketch decoding; familiar-fallback specificity concerns familiar examples sent to fallback. The activity does not state the measured values.
When you say “measure its routing,” are we checking the logical forms it produces?

Not in these two measures. They check which path the gate selects for each kind of example. Withheld-sketch recall asks how often withheld combinations go to sketch decoding, and familiar-fallback specificity asks how often familiar examples go to fallback. Neither measure, by itself, says whether a resulting logical form is an exact match.
What does “on ScopeBind-Match” modify here?

It identifies ScopeBind-Match as the setting for training the typed-signature gate. The measurements are to be made on matched test splits. This activity does not specify the gate’s training objective or further details about how the splits are constructed.
Are the test splits matched for the same things we discussed before?

Yes. In the established plan, ScopeBind-Match splits are vocabulary- and length-matched. Referring to matched test splits here carries forward those stated matching conditions, without adding a requirement that each individual sentence have an identical counterpart.
Why measure withheld-sketch recall on the test splits instead of merely checking whether the gate has a sketch route?

Having a sketch route would establish only that the route exists. Measuring withheld-sketch recall asks how often the trained gate actually selects it for withheld scope–binding combinations in the matched test splits. That is the behavior at issue, though the activity supplies no result yet.
And what exactly gets counted for familiar-fallback specificity?

It counts familiar examples in the matched test splits that the gate sends to fallback, relative to the familiar examples being assessed. It is a group-specific routing measure, not a measure of the fallback’s logical-form accuracy.
Does this activity already tell us whether the proposed 95% and 98% routing thresholds are met?

No. Training the gate and measuring the two quantities is the activity needed to obtain evidence relevant to those thresholds. No measured recall or specificity is given here, so there is no stated pass or fail for either one.
Could I report the two values together as one accuracy number?

That would obscure the distinction the activity is meant to measure. Withheld-sketch recall and familiar-fallback specificity concern different sets of examples and different destinations. The activity calls for both measures, not a single combined value in their place.
What if the gate routes a withheld combination to sketch decoding but the sketch decoder later makes a binding error?

That case would still count as routed to sketch decoding for withheld-sketch recall. A later binding error concerns the parser’s output, which this gate measurement does not establish. Keeping routing and logical-form correctness separate is important here.
Likewise, sending a familiar example to fallback does not establish that fallback got it right?

Correct. Familiar-fallback specificity concerns the gate’s destination choice. It does not show that the fallback returned the correct logical form or that the complete parser meets the familiar-construction exact-match requirement.
Does saying “train the gate” imply a particular way of deriving typed signatures?

No. The activity names the typed-signature gate and says to train it on ScopeBind-Match, but it gives no signature derivation procedure or training recipe. Those details should remain unspecified rather than being read into the activity.
So this is an evaluation of the gate hypothesis, but not yet an evaluation result?

Yes. Measuring withheld-sketch recall and familiar-fallback specificity on matched test splits is how this activity examines the gate’s predicted routing behavior. The activity describes what to train and measure; it does not claim the prediction is supported or refuted.
Can you restate the activity without making it sound completed?

Train the typed-signature gate on ScopeBind-Match, then measure withheld-sketch recall and familiar-fallback specificity on matched test splits. Reported measurements or conclusions are not part of this activity statement.
On ScopeBind-Match, the gate achieved 83% withheld-sketch recall versus the 95% target, despite 99% familiar-fallback specificity.

The result is uneven across the two routing measures. On withheld combinations, the gate sent 83% to sketch decoding, 12 percentage points below the stated 95% target. Familiar-fallback specificity was 99%, meaning 99% of familiar examples were routed to fallback. These are gate-routing results, not logical-form exact-match results.
When you say 83% withheld-sketch recall, what is the denominator?

The denominator is the withheld scope–binding combinations assessed on ScopeBind-Match. The 83% is the share of those combinations routed to sketch decoding, not the share of all examples routed there.
Does the 99% figure use that same denominator?

No. Familiar-fallback specificity is measured over familiar examples. Its 99% figure is the share of familiar examples sent to fallback, so the two percentages describe routing behavior on different groups.
Is the difference between 83% and 95% twelve percent or twelve percentage points?
Twelve percentage points. The direct difference between the two stated percentages is 95% minus 83%, or 12 percentage points. That wording does not imply a particular relative percentage change.
How should I understand the word “despite” in the result?

It highlights a contrast: the gate routed familiar examples to fallback at 99%, yet its withheld-sketch recall was 83% against the 95% target. Strong routing to fallback for familiar examples does not, by itself, ensure that withheld combinations are routed to sketch decoding at the desired rate.
Does the result tell us where withheld examples went when they did not reach sketch decoding?

It tells us they were not counted among the withheld examples routed to sketch decoding. The evidence does not specify their destinations or give a breakdown of other routing outcomes, so I would not assign those examples to a particular path from this result alone.
Can we tell whether the typed signatures failed to represent binding properly?

No cause is established by these two measurements. They report how the gate routed the two groups, but they do not identify why withheld-sketch recall was 83%. In particular, they do not isolate the signatures’ representation of binding as the cause.
Could the 99% familiar-fallback specificity make up for the withheld-sketch recall gap?

Not for the withheld-sketch recall measure. Familiar-fallback specificity and withheld-sketch recall have different denominators and destinations. The 99% observation does not change the fact that withheld-sketch recall was 83% versus its 95% target.
Does 83% withheld-sketch recall mean 83% logical-form exact match on withheld combinations?

No. It means 83% were routed to sketch decoding. The evidence does not say how many logical forms produced by sketch decoding, or by any other route, exactly matched their references. Routing recall and end-to-end logical-form accuracy should not be equated.
And does 99% specificity tell us familiar-construction exact-match accuracy?

No. It says how often familiar examples reached fallback, not whether the fallback produced the correct logical form. It cannot by itself establish a familiar-construction exact-match score or the comparison with an equally sized supervised baseline.
Does vocabulary and length matching explain the 83% figure?

The ScopeBind-Match setting uses vocabulary- and length-matched splits, which defines the context for the measurement. Matching those distributions does not, by itself, explain why the gate obtained 83% withheld-sketch recall. The reported evidence gives the result, not a causal account of it.
Can we infer an overall gate accuracy from the two figures?

Not from these figures alone. An overall value would depend in part on how the groups are combined and on what counts as correct routing across the assessed examples. The evidence reports the two group-specific measures instead.
What is the most careful way to report this evidence without adding a diagnosis?

On ScopeBind-Match, the gate achieved 83% withheld-sketch recall, 12 percentage points below its 95% target, despite 99% familiar-fallback specificity. These figures describe routing; they do not report logical-form accuracy or explain the recall gap.

I have a hypothesis about the routing question: a novelty gate over canonical quantifier–binder graphs will achieve at least 95% withheld-sketch recall while retaining at least 98% familiar-fallback specificity.

That is a prediction about two routing measures. The hypothesized gate would send ≥95% of withheld scope–binding combinations to sketch decoding and ≥98% of familiar examples to fallback. The statement does not establish that either rate has been achieved.
What does “novelty gate” mean in this hypothesis?

In broad terms, it is a gate intended to distinguish novel scope–binding compositions from familiar ones for routing purposes. Here, the proposed basis for that distinction is canonical quantifier–binder graphs. The hypothesis does not specify the gate’s exact decision rule.
What is a quantifier–binder graph supposed to capture?

Conceptually, it represents relationships relevant to quantifier scope and variable binding in graph form. Calling the graphs “canonical” suggests a consistent representation for comparison. The hypothesis does not define the graph format, its canonicalization procedure, or how a graph is obtained from an input.
Does canonical mean we can assume any two sentences with the same meaning have identical graphs?

No. That would be a stronger property than the hypothesis states. “Canonical” is part of the proposed representation’s name, but no precise equivalence criterion or guarantee about meaning-identical sentences is given.
How does this relate to distinguishing withheld combinations when vocabulary and sentence length are matched?

The hypothesis places the routing distinction in quantifier–binder structure, rather than treating vocabulary or length as the distinguishing signal. Matching vocabulary and sentence length does not itself determine whether such a gate succeeds. The predicted recall and specificity are the claims that would need to be assessed under those conditions.
Could “novelty” just mean the gate notices a word it has never seen?

That would not express the stated hypothesis well. The proposed gate operates over canonical quantifier–binder graphs, and the relevant novelty concerns withheld scope–binding combinations. The hypothesis does not make unfamiliar words its criterion.
What exactly would count toward the 95% figure?

A withheld combination counts toward withheld-sketch recall if the gate routes it to sketch decoding. The hypothesis predicts that this happens for at least 95% of withheld combinations. That percentage has withheld combinations as its denominator.
What counts toward the 98% figure?
